title: Steve Jobs in Exile
summary: We all know the Steve Jobs who came back in the late 1990s and saved Apple from becoming a footnote. And we’ve all heard the story of how, in 1985, he was pushed out of the company he’d created. What we don’t know is what happened in between. Geoffrey Cain spent years reconstructing the decade … The post Steve Jobs in Exile appeared first on Farnam Street .
content:
We all know the Steve Jobs who came back in the late 1990s and saved Apple from becoming a footnote. And we’ve all heard the story of how, in 1985, he was pushed out of the company he’d created.

What we don’t know is what happened in between.

Geoffrey Cain spent years reconstructing the decade Jobs spent outside Apple. NeXT spent years losing money. His co-founders left. His investors lost faith. His fortune nearly disappeared. At one point, he was a weekend away from shutting the company down.

Somewhere in those failures, Jobs learned how to become the leader Apple would eventually need.

This is Steve Jobs before he became Steve Jobs.

Listen and Learn: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Members get the longer version of this conversation, plus additional content not included in the public release.

Tiny Lessons

Ego, Product, and the Market

  • “Here’s what I learned about his reality distortion field, and this is what made it so dangerous. It wasn’t just about convincing other people that his ideas were infallible. It was also about convincing himself.”
  • “Steve originally thought that a great idea was what mattered. If you build the great computer, the world will find it, buy it, and you will be a success. But that’s not how the world works.”
  • “You can go up there and take potshots at each other in public, but that’s not going to drive sales. It won’t make your product more interesting to people. It’s certainly a spectacle, and it’s theater, but ultimately, it’s the product that matters.”
  • You have to meet the market where it is.

Leadership and Talent

  • “Something interesting happens when you’re the CEO leading great people, when you have talent around. The pyramid gets inverted. You’re no longer the boss up top telling people what to do. You are the CEO at the bottom, and your job is to allow your talent to do their best and to keep them around, because your talent can get another job in a minute, so you better do what you can to keep them around, or else you’re going to fail.”
  • “Talk back and disagree with me, and we’ll find the answer through disagreement.”
  • “You do have to step back, and you have to let events unfold as they need to, rather than you trying to seize control at every moment.”
  • “You can’t do everything just because you think it’s a neat idea. You have to focus your efforts on what will be profitable.”
  • Pushing talented people toward standards higher than they think they can reach brings out the best in them.

Pragmatism and Strategy

  • “Even if you disagree with them, even if you think their taste sucks, and you think that their products are terrible, if they have a pot of money, and they can help you, you have to do the handshake.”
  • “You have to make concessions. You can’t do everything exactly as you start out planning to.”
  • The difference between a visionary and a failure is knowing when to stick to your guns and knowing when to bend your vision to work with the world around you.

Resilience and the Wilderness

  • Failure doesn’t matter: “He was resilient in the face of failure after failure. Once he learned discipline, his resilience became the foundation for his success.”
  • “If you’re in hard times, you treat it as the foundation for what might come after. That’s where the resilience comes from. If you’re only focused on the current moment, then it’s easy to give up. But failure could be the foundation for success later.”
  • “In the wilderness years, those are hard years, but that’s where many great leaders have learned to become who they need to be.”
  • “Steve learned the power of inspiring the people around him, but he never completely learned to be 100% honest with himself.”

Transcript

Shane Parrish: Everybody knows about Steve Jobs. The legend, the myth, the man who shows us the future, but very few people see this period where he walks through the wilderness, and fails over and over again. And I want to talk about that with you today.

Geoffrey Cain: Looking forward to it, Shane.

Shane Parrish: I think the right place to start is leading up to the original, I wouldn’t say firing, but the original leaving from Apple, and the coup attempt with Sculley. And can you walk me through what happened in the year or two leading up to that that led to that?

Geoffrey Cain: Steve Jobs was a brilliant young man. He was a visionary. He co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak in his garage. And in 1984, he released the Macintosh computer. This was game-changing, because you have to remember, in the 1980s, using a computer was really difficult.

A lot of them were the size of a room, and the whole idea of a personal computer that sits on your desk was entirely new. Steve took the technology of the past, and made it available to everybody. He called it the bicycle for the mind. The Macintosh, it was a cultural success. It was out there. People were talking about it, but the reality is that it was not a commercial success. It just wasn’t selling.

And so, because sales were weak, Apple entered a crisis in 1985, a year after the Macintosh was released. And meanwhile, Steve had brought on John Sculley, the CEO of Apple. He was going to provide adult supervision.

And so, he would be the guy who would turn Apple from a scrappy little startup into an actual corporation. But, this did not go as planned for Steve. Because of all these failures with the Macintosh, Apple was just not really doing that well anymore.

There were debts piling up. They had to lay off workers for the first time in 1985. And then, finally, when all of this reached a head, Steve just found himself being pushed out of the company. He was impossible to manage. He was extremely difficult.

He was so convinced of his own brilliance, and he was brilliant, but so convinced of his brilliance that he would storm into meetings, he would yell at people, he would tell them, “You’re not doing your job right.” And they would say, “Steve, you’re not even my boss.” One of the things that we often forget about Steve Jobs is that he was not the CEO of Apple.

He ran the Macintosh division, so his job was simply to build the Macintosh. Apple got a lot of complaints. They went up to John Sculley, the CEO. John was getting tired of him, because he could not manage Steve. And so in the end, they made the decision that Steve has to do something else for a while. Steve actually tried to launch a coup d’etat against the CEO, John Sculley.

It was early 1985, and he said, “Here’s what I’m going to do. It’s a plot. I’m going to get a speaking gig in China. And then John Sculley, once I tell him, he’s going to want to join me too.” Steve invited him out, and then Steve bailed, said, “I have other plans.” And then, the plan was that Steve was going to walk into the boardroom when John Sculley was gone, and tell them that John had to be ousted. And he wanted the board to make him the CEO. Steve Jobs tried to become the CEO of Apple, but he failed. He wasn’t ready.

Shane Parrish: He led Sculley to believe that he was on the flight. Somebody told Sculley that he wasn’t going, and then he showed up at the meeting the next day, and Sculley was there, and that forced the decision.

Geoffrey Cain: Yes. Steve Jobs had a rival named Jean-Louis Gassée. And Gassée was the head of Apple France, very successful in the company, and was being groomed to be the next Steve Jobs. He was going to come in, he was going to run the Macintosh. And so, Steve decided to tell Jean-Louis Gassée about his plot. He met him in the parking lot.

He said, “Here’s what I’m going to do. I’m going to overthrow the CEO of Apple.” And so, Jean-Louis Gassée, that night is at the CEO’s house, and pulls him aside, and says, “I got to tell you about what Steve Jobs is going to do to you. If you go to China, you might not have a job anymore.”

Shane Parrish: One of the battles going on at the time, if my memory serves me correct, is the open Macintosh computer, or Mac, what was it called, the Mac 2?

Geoffrey Cain: Yes, the Macintosh 2.

Shane Parrish: Yeah, so the open one that Wozniak had created where people could put their own components in, take it apart, that was keeping them afloat. And Steve’s version of the computer, which was closed, and more controlled, which is a theme I think we’re going to talk about a lot today, was the reason that Apple was facing financial struggles because it wasn’t selling.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. Steve, he did have a brilliant vision. He wanted a computer to be an end-to-end product. The same company he thought should control everything from the hardware, to the components, to the software, the mouse, the keyboard, everything, which is like what the iPhone is today. The problem though is that in the 1980s, this was not a practical way of doing business. A lot of consumers were business consumers.

They would have a nice big PC in their office, and they could take out cards, and take out slots. They could customize it however they needed. That’s what the world wanted, but Steve failed to see that at the time. He thought that his vision was so smart that people would beat down a door to buy his computers even if they were closed. But, he quickly realized that that’s not what the world actually wanted.

Shane Parrish: This will come back again in this story. He gets ousted. He leaves Apple. He’s very well off. He’s got over $100,000,000, I think. And then, what happens next?

Geoffrey Cain: It’s September 1985. He has spent the summer in Europe. And so, this is the summer where he’s really getting a taste, his first taste of what it’s like to be without Apple. And you have to remember, Steve’s an intense guy. He was spending long nights, long days. His whole life was Apple, and people around him remarked that he didn’t have any real friends.

Shane Parrish: He probably had no identity either, right? Because all of his identity was tied to being the co-founder of Apple.

Geoffrey Cain: Absolutely. His entire identity, his being was Apple. And so, having that torn away from him, being pushed out and told, “You’re not needed here anymore,” what they did is they gave him a new made up unit, and they said, “You leave, so you’re not going to work on the Macintosh anymore, which is your baby.” That was his creation. And they say, “You’re going to get a lonely office across the street.”

He nicknamed it Siberia, and then everybody just ignored him. It was the fall of Steve Jobs that entire summer. And then, finally, he said, “I’m headed off to Europe. I can’t take this anymore.” And so, he spent that whole summer, this winding summer of just exploration, of looking at paintings and museums, and going to coffee shops. This was a rare moment when he had to stop, and he had to reflect and look inward, and figure out what he was doing wrong. And so, in the end, Steve decided that he could not stay at Apple.

Shane Parrish: Was he reflecting on what he did wrong in 1985, or did he more take the approach of they’re wrong, they just don’t see what a genius I am?

Geoffrey Cain: It’s the second one. He took the approach of, I did nothing wrong here. I tried to oust the CEO, but that’s because the CEO is an idiot. That was his thinking. He didn’t realize that for him to stay at Apple, he was going to have to produce something that would sell. That was the bottom line. His computers weren’t selling.

Shane Parrish: Okay, so what happens next? He comes back from Europe.

Geoffrey Cain: He decides that he’s going to leave Apple, and he wants to go into the next phase of his career. He’s 30 years old, and he says, “I am going to make the most cutting-edge computer for the leading science laboratories, the university departments. I’m going to make the best computer that can be possibly available on the market, and it’s going to be a computer that’s going to allow students in dorm rooms to cure cancer.”

But, there’s a problem. To make that, he’s going to have to poach five Apple employees, and these ones are especially talented. He goes in, he tells John Sculley, the CEO, “I’m taking these five with me.” John Sculley freaks out. What Apple does next is one of the most dramatic things I’ve seen a company do to one of its co-founders, they decide to sue him.

Shane Parrish: In an effort to prevent him from starting, or to control what he does when he starts?

Geoffrey Cain: It’s both. They don’t want him to start the new company. The way that Apple looked at Steve was a bit schizophrenic in a way. He was the spiritual heart of the company, and it was in many ways his company. There’s no Apple without Steve Jobs. But then, the other worry, they accused him of stealing intellectual property.

Shane Parrish: Of course.

Geoffrey Cain: Steve was working on a new computer at Apple. It’s called the 3M Machine. And the 3M Machine, it’s this idea of a supercomputer essentially, so more powerful than a Macintosh, more powerful than the typical PC of the day. But, that would be the kind of computer that could be used for scientists, and researchers, and also intelligence agencies. And so, Steve decides that this is the computer he’s going to make at his new company, which he calls NeXT computer.

Shane Parrish: And so, he takes these five co-founders with him, he starts NeXT, and then, he’s spending money like crazy at this point. And I think there’s a logo story. Tell me the logo story.

Geoffrey Cain: Steve is such a perfectionist. He’s a man of high taste. And especially from the fortune he had built at Apple, he had really gotten that champagne taste, and he only wanted the best. This is the opposite of the younger Steve, the guy in the garage with the holes in his jeans and hadn’t showered for days, who washes his feet in the toilet. That’s that Steve.

But, this is Steve at 30, and now he’s elevating his surroundings. He’s starting to realize that since he’s no longer building a startup, that’s not how he sees it. He wants to start at the top shelf. And so, one of the first things that Steve does is he sets out to craft a logo. He only wants the best logo from the best graphic designer in the country, a man named Paul Rand. And so, Steve approaches Paul Rand, and says, “I want you to give me the best logo you can.” And Paul Rand’s response is, “You’ll pay me $100,000 for the logo. You only get one shot, and you can’t change your mind. That’s that. No questions asked.”

Shane Parrish: Whether you use the logo or not, and $100,000 at the time, it’s a lot of money now, but at the time, it’s like an insane amount of money.

Geoffrey Cain: Even today, that’s an insane amount of money for a startup. And in 1985 and ’86, the number is astronomical. And so, people are looking at this and scratching their heads and saying, “So what exactly is Steve Jobs doing?” And this logo, it’s a classic. People still study it. Design schools still study it.

But at the time, people were wondering, “Well, what does this mean for the company expenses?” And so, as a result of spending $100,000 on a logo, company expenses suddenly become pegged to $100,000. And meanwhile, Steve has invested $7 million of his own money in NeXT computer. When every expenditure is $100,000, and you’re only running on $7 million without a product, it’s three years until release, you’re already in trouble.

Steve started off on the wrong foot. He did get a beautiful logo, but he was too far ahead of the market, and what the market wanted from him.

Shane Parrish: And he wanted the computer to be beautiful in and of itself. There’s a whole story around The Cube.

Geoffrey Cain: The Cube was a perfect object that Steve wanted to create. And so, he wanted his computer to be literally a perfect Cube, 90 degree angles, so it’s a beautiful item, absolutely gorgeous. But, manufacturing it is just a pain in the neck. It’s almost impossible. And so, they had to go to a specialist mold shop.

They had a special sanding line. It was a $500,000 sanding line in 1986 that would sand every computer. Steve, in deciding that he wanted to build a perfect Cube for a computer, he’s automatically added millions of dollars in expenses that are going to accrue over time just by choosing a perfect Cube.

In the end, Steve had created this masterpiece of art, this masterpiece of technology, but it was so impractical that the cost was just going to get out of control.

Shane Parrish: It was so expensive, he priced himself out of the market.

Geoffrey Cain: Right at the start. He priced himself out of the market, because he predicted that everybody’s going to want to buy this. They’re going to see how smart Steve Jobs is. And then, Steve is going to be proven right in the end. He’s going to get back at Apple, and have an even cooler computer than Apple does.

Shane Parrish: This reminds me of something John Mackey told me when I was interviewing him, the founder of Whole Foods. And he said you have to meet the market where it is.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. The market for a $10,000 computer in 1986, a perfect Cube that looks gorgeous, is extremely, extremely niche. And even today, no person in their right mind would actually buy this thing.

Shane Parrish: And are people giving him feedback that like, “No, you shouldn’t be doing this,” or, “This is too expensive, or nobody will buy this,” or is it the classic story of nobody wanted to give Steve bad news?

Geoffrey Cain: This is one of the surprising things I found. I always assumed that people were scared of Steve Jobs, and he would yell at them, and curse, and they would just go quiet and run away. That’s something that we see in movies, but that’s actually not how things played out in real life. Steve hired people because he wanted them to talk back.

He wanted people with edge. He would go out there, he would pose these really hard interview questions. He would say, “Are you the best person in your field?” And if you hesitated, or said, “I don’t know,” he would say, “Well, the interview’s over. I only want to talk to the number one person, so go find them for me and then we’ll talk.”

And it just shows that’s what Steve wanted. He wanted people who would defend themselves, defend their ideas. They weren’t afraid to stand up to him and say, “Hey, Steve, let’s do it this way.”

One of the reasons Steve would be so difficult with people was because he was trying to get them to push back. He was saying, “I have this force of personality, and I want you to show me why your idea is not totally stupid, please.” That was the idea.

Shane Parrish: I love that. And in terms of challenging people, even if he believed them, he just wanted to see that they believed in their own ideas, that they had thought things through.

Geoffrey Cain: Right, right. You’re going to stand up to yourself. Also, you’re going to engage in intellectual combat. That’s what he wanted. Not just combat with Steve, but intellectual combat with the whole team. They would all get together in a room with Steve. Steve liked to hold these retreats. They would go stay at a nice hotel and gather in the conference room. And Steve would come out and say, “Okay, so give me your best ideas.” And then, everybody, the software team, the hardware team, the marketing team, the sales team, they would all have to stand up one by one, and fight for what they believed in.

And if Steve though they weren’t fighting enough, he would push them harder. He would say, “No, this is not good enough. It’s really not good enough.” They were not scared of Steve. They were not cowering in front of him. They were telling Steve exactly what was going to happen. And they would tell him, “Steve, you hired me, because I’m the best software developer. I’m the best in my field, and I’m telling you that this is not going to work.” And Steve ignored them anyway.

Shane Parrish: Why was he ignoring them?

Geoffrey Cain: I think that he was trying to build a monument to his own genius. Steve was really immature at this stage in his life. I saw emails where his executives would give him the numbers and say, “Look, literally, if you don’t raise this much money by this date, and sell this many Cube computers, the company’s going to fail.”

And Steve would say, “Well, we don’t have to worry about that because we’re going to sell 25,000 computers this year.” And they would say, “Steve, we’re not going to sell that, because we don’t even have a distribution network set up. There’s literally no one selling the computer out there for us, so how are we going to sell it?” And he would say, “I know it’s going to work, because I tried it today, and it’s a great computer. It’s a great product, so of course it’s going to work.”

Shane Parrish: Is this the reality distortion field where he’s not allowing anything into his perception, and then trying to create a picture of something that’s completely untrue? Did he know he was lying or did he actually believe it?

Geoffrey Cain: I think he actually believed it. I think that he did say things that he did not know for sure to be true, but I don’t think he ever saw himself as outright lying. Here’s what I learned about his reality distortion field, and this is what made it so dangerous. It wasn’t just about convincing other people that his ideas were infallible.

It was also about convincing himself. And he would listen to people sometimes, but other times, if it clashed too much with his vision, he would dismiss them. His biggest fault was building a monument to his own genius, his own vision, and thinking that that would be enough for the market and enough to beat Apple and get revenge on Apple.

Shane Parrish: The NeXTcube played a huge role in the internet with Tim Berners-Lee, but nobody even wanted to tell Steve Jobs. What is that story?

Geoffrey Cain: The world wide web was created on a NeXT computer.

Shane Parrish: That’s insane.

Geoffrey Cain: It’s insane. It’s a forgotten story. That’s how good these computers were. The software especially, these computers arrived on the desk of Tim Berners-Lee. And he wrote about it later about just how revolutionary the software was, how if he had tried to create the web without a NeXT computer, it would’ve taken so much more time, months, maybe years more. But, he was able to code the web, and create the web in a really short amount of time.

It was in late 1990 using object-oriented programming. Literally at one point, the entire worldwide web was housed on a single computer that Tim Berners-Lee was using at CERN, the laboratory in Europe. And there was even a sign on it. There are photos of this computer, and he scribbled this funny sticker on it that says, “This is a server. Do not power it down.” If anybody came along like a cleaner and accidentally unplugged it or something, the entire worldwide web would’ve gone down right there. And that’s how rudimentary this technology was at the time.

Shane Parrish: Nobody wanted to tell Steve Jobs that this had been done on a NeXT computer. That struck me as fascinating.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. The web was not seen as revolutionary at the time.

Shane Parrish: The most revolutionary human that we’ve known in computers who’s got probably the most vision, but Steve doesn’t see the web. He doesn’t see it coming. He’s got a big blind spot around it and nobody wants to tell him about it.

Geoffrey Cain: They’re all afraid that Steve’s going to say it’s shit. That’s what Steve would call stuff that he didn’t like. But, Steve had a habit of doing that. They would bring an idea to him and he would say, “This is shit” They just didn’t want to deal with the difficulty of presenting something to Steve.

Shane Parrish: That’s insane. And so, he’s not learning, but he’s getting a lot of feedback. The moment of learning I think is the hardware division failure. That’s his lowest point. Walk me through this.

Geoffrey Cain: That is Steve Jobs at rock bottom, and that is a Steve Jobs that we’ve almost never seen before.

Shane Parrish: What happened?

Geoffrey Cain: Steve was piling up debts. He was refusing to kill the hardware division, so the NeXTcube was not succeeding. The sales were just a few dozen a month. It was ridiculous. I even looked at the numbers and I though, how could any business survive with this? And so, instead of killing the hardware, Steve kept going around to different investors and saying, “We have something great coming. Invest a bunch of money.” He went to Canon. Canon gave him $100 million and got a board seat.

Ross Perot, his other investor, Ross Perot got a board seat, and invested $20 million at the start. These investors were surrounding him, and the effect was interesting. The effect was magical thinking. And as a result of Canon investing, and Ross Perot investing, and IBM set up a deal, that automatically raised the valuation of NeXT and gave it credibility.

Even though the whole company was smoke and mirrors, they were still raising more and more money, so they were creating a bubble. The NeXT hardware was not selling. Steve would not give it up. And then, finally, in 1993, the company was on the verge of bankruptcy, literally one weekend away from just closing the doors completely.

And so, Steve Jobs and his hardware chief, John Rubinstein, who was also one of the creators of the iPhone later, called up Canon, their investor, and said, “It’s a cramdown. Give us $20 million now, or else we’re closing.” And so, the Canon investors said, “Well, I guess, we have no choice here because we’re going to lose all of our investments if this company goes up in smoke.”

Shane Parrish: Leading up to this the 1990 -1993, the software was getting really good. When it first came out, it was pretty buggy, but everybody loved their software. And the hardware division is what’s killing it, but IBM wanted to license just their software, didn’t they?

Geoffrey Cain: Right. NeXT computer was revolutionary in its software. The hardware was the failure. And we look at the hardware and think, oh, this company failed. But, the software is where the future actually lived. And this is where the vision and the future forward-looking of Steve Jobs comes in.

He was working on software in 1986, that by the year 2007, would be the foundation of the iPhone. That’s how far ahead of his time he was. He had come upon a relatively novel technology called object-oriented programming.

For anybody who wasn’t an adult in the 1980s who doesn’t remember what it was like using a computer, if you wanted to develop an app, or basically do anything significant, it took a ton of code. You had to go through line by line of code, and it was inefficient. There would be one mistake in there, and then that one mistake would just crash the whole system.

And then, you had to go back through the whole thing, start over. Programming a computer was miserable. Steve, from his visits to Xerox PARC, saw what was called object-oriented programming, which is the foundation for Apple products now.

This is the drag and drop, so this is everything is an object, so you might have the button object, the click here object. You might have the image object, the menu object. You have all these things that are on the screen, and you can rearrange them, and make them work together.

Object-oriented programming was automation for software. It was roughly the equivalent of the industrial revolution for hardware, the cogs, the perpetual motion, the stuff that just moves on the factory line. That was the hardware revolution. The software revolution was objects. And that was there are all these objects I have on the screen. I’m going to sculpt it like clay, and turn it into beautiful software as opposed to clunky old software that’s just really hard to put together.

Shane Parrish: He was building software at the time using drag and drop like all of NeXT was, but the problem is they had no install base, so nobody else is building software for NeXT, so there’s no reason to purchase NeXT because it’s a very niche market.

Geoffrey Cain: Steve made that mistake early on, because he wanted to, once again, control the hardware and the software together. NeXTSTEP was the name of his operating system. This is the operating system that tapped into the power of objects. But, the problem was that it was confined to his NeXT hardware, which no one wanted to buy, because it was too expensive.

Over time, a lot of customers, clients came into the office and said, “Look, Steve, the reason we’re buying your beautiful Cube computers is not because it’s a beautiful Cube. Nobody cares about that. We’re buying it, because we want to use your powerful software for financial trades, ahead of its time. Speedy financial trades back when this is a new thing, we want to buy it for healthcare.”

Satellite imagery, intelligence work. The CIA loved it. The NSA loved it. It had a removable optical disc, a new thing at the time that the CIA agents could destroy, and toss out, so nobody could find it. It really was a machine that was ahead of its time. The hardware was just so unworkable, because it was so far into the future. But, the software was where the real power was here.

Shane Parrish: But, he was playing on hard mode, right? He had opportunities in front of him. IBM came to him wanting to give him money and license software. The government was trying to buy a whole bunch of computers. Walk me through those two stories where he self-sabotages.

Geoffrey Cain: He totally self-sabotaged. And the whole world would look different today if this had gone in a different route. This is one of the stories that blows my mind about Steve Jobs. Ross Perot is his investor. Ross Perot, for people who don’t remember, he was a technology magnet from Texas, a billionaire, one of the greatest investors of his era, also ran for president twice on an independent ticket. This is who Steve Jobs brings on board.

And everybody who worked with the two said it was a really funny pairing, because Steve is ‘Mr. Birkenstock’s California Mystic’. And then, Ross Perot, the straight laced Texas, the military veteran who’s going to run for president. These two guys were so far apart that it should have been obvious that it wasn’t going to work out in the end.

One of the handshake deals of this partnership is that Ross Perot promises to mobilize his sales force to sell NeXT computers to the federal government, the military, and intelligence agencies.

And so, there are intelligence contractors and spies coming around during these years to the NeXT headquarters. These guys would show up. I heard really funny stories. They would never carry a business card, and they would say, “Hey, my name is Sally. My name’s Bob.” They wouldn’t ever say their real name. And Steve decided in the end that he doesn’t want to sell to the federal government, because that’s not who Steve is. He’s all about democratizing computers. He wanted to sell to schools, to dorm room students. That’s the sort of audience that he goes after.

But, Steve blew this up, and it was a disaster because he had millions, hundreds of millions potentially in government contracts being lined up for him. And then, he said, “I don’t want to do this. I changed my mind. I don’t want to sell to the feds, so Ross, I’m not doing this.” And this blew up their relationship. Ross quit. He was so frustrated, so angry with Steve.

Shane Parrish: They were literally at the boardroom table with the contracts.

Geoffrey Cain: They were literally at the table ready to sign the contract. And Steve said, “I’m not doing this.”

Shane Parrish: I just want to give people context here. We’re in 1993 at this point. The hardware division has just been bankrupt. He goes to Canon. He’s like, “I need $20 million by Monday, or else we’re shutting the doors to the whole company.” He’s refused to sell to government despite them trying to give him money, literally lining up to give him enough money to more than stay afloat.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. Steve was alone. He was completely alone. He had driven out his co-founders. All five of them had left, because they were so tired of working with Steve. He had alienated all of his investors. Canon, his only remaining investor, was no longer responding to his emails. His developers were all out. They said, “I’m tired of this. I’m not going to develop software for a machine that no one’s using, a machine that is now closed and failing.”

This was Steve at rock bottom. And even Fortune magazine published this article, and said, “Steve Jobs might be a snake oil salesman.” They used that exact phrase, snake oil salesman for Steve Jobs. When I was looking at Steve Jobs at rock bottom, I thought, oh my God, this is the Steve Jobs we never see. You never see Steve being accused of being a scammer. You never see Steve almost bankrupt.

He was almost personally out of money. He was burning through about $50 million a year, according to the people who knew him. And he was investing his own money into these businesses, because he didn’t want to take them public. And so, if the businesses went under, then Steve Jobs would go under. And he was very close to being completely forgotten and written out of history.

Shane Parrish: Was he funding Pixar at the same time? When did Pixar come into the picture?

Geoffrey Cain: Steve Jobs was personally funding two companies, NeXT Computer and Pixar from 1985 to 1995. In late 1995, Pixar had its IPO because of Toy Story, which was a major success. And that’s actually what saved Steve in the end financially. He became a billionaire as a result of that IPO that might have never happened.

Shane Parrish: That’s crazy. He’s funding both of these companies, he’s running out of cash. What changes in that moment, because that’s the lowest point. That’s where everything turns around in this whole story, and he starts to become the legend of Steve Jobs that we know and love.

Geoffrey Cain: It’s the realization that he’s alone, and almost a complete failure in business. It’s also his marriage to Laurene, and having children with her that started to rehabilitate him. He started to realize that there are bigger and greater things out there when it comes to starting a family and having kids.

These moments, it was these years, 1993 to ’95 that were enormously transformative for him, both professionally and personally. And having Laurene around really started to tame him, make him mature, also realizing that he had to back off.

One of the reasons Pixar was successful was because Steve was not involved day to day. The deal that they had, Steve bought Pixar from George Lucas, and the deal, the agreement was Steve stays out of creative decisions. That’s going to make things easier for us. Ed Catmull, John Lasseter, two luminaries at Pixar, they were the ones who actually made the creative stuff happen.

Most people don’t realize that Steve Jobs was credited as a producer of Toy Story, but the reason you don’t realize that is because he wasn’t really the face of the project anymore. It wasn’t like the Apple where you saw Steve and Apple together. You can’t separate the two. But, with Pixar, once he backed off, things worked great.

Steve did what he did best. He would give the presentations, convince people to invest. He would eventually sell Pixar to Disney, a brilliant master stroke of business. But, the creative hands were left to do what they did best. And so, Steve learned to finally trust people.

Shane Parrish: He steps back a little bit from NeXT. Is that-

Geoffrey Cain: He stepped back not just a little bit, he stepped back by a wide gaping margin. He realized just how damaging his actions had been, just how damaging his need for total control was. And so, he allowed his executives at NeXT to take over. One of the things that NeXT executives quickly realized is that the only way to save the company, which was $400 million in debt …

Remember, this is a small startup that hasn’t even produced a successful product in nine years. It’s literally been making a loss for nine years. The moment he hires some real financial professionals, there was a new CFO named Dominique Trempont who is from Belgium, and came in, and looked at the situation, and said, “This is pretty bad. I don’t know if we can save this place, but we’ll do what we can.”

The moment that that team came in, and looked at the books, and told Steve what they need to do, that’s when things changed. And now, NeXT, for the first time ever, in the year 1994, posted a very small profit, and finally came out of that nine years of endless unprofitability, and finally was starting to look like a real business once ironically, Steve Jobs was gone.

Shane Parrish: Was he gone, or was he just more hands-off?

Geoffrey Cain: He was gone in the sense that he went to Pixar more. Pixar became his baby. He loved Toy Story, which they were creating at the time. He really loved this idea of technology being used to create beautiful cultural items. What NeXT Computer was doing, the only way that they could survive was by creating enterprise software.

Shane Parrish: And he had no interest in that.

Geoffrey Cain: He was like, “I’m not doing that. Why would I do that? I’m going to sell the NeXT great computer to the next Nobel winning scientist. That’s what the company is.” But, once his financial advisors said, “Look, if you don’t change this, it’s going to go under. You’re $400 million in debt. You have no choice.” Steve backed off. He was not interested in enterprise computing.

Come on, Steve Jobs? You watch the events that he gave the product launches during this time, and he does not look like Steve Jobs at all. He’s not wearing that black turtleneck. He doesn’t have the scruffy beard. He doesn’t have the glasses. He’s wearing an Armani suit, with a white buttoned down shirt, and a red tie. And at one point, he even gave an interview and he said, “The future of our company is going to be like IBM.”

Shane Parrish: This is like ’93 to ’95.

Geoffrey Cain: He’s Steve Jobs, the corporate salesman, walking around the conference room floor, with his conservative dapper suit, and shaking hands and saying, “Hello, would you like to buy my enterprise software? Are you a financial firm on Wall Street? We can sell to you.”

Shane Parrish: Oh, my God. That’s amazing. And so, Pixar IPOs, and that gives Steve a lot of financial freedom. Really gives him leverage over the Apple transaction, which is coming. But, at the time, Apple was struggling, so it’s important to contextualize this, I think. Why are they struggling? What’s going on at Apple?

Geoffrey Cain: Apple grew into a big corporation, and like many successful startups that grow, it got featuritis, as they call it. It got the syndrome of bureaucracy, the syndromes of making too many products, of having too many people, too many offices, too many titles.

By the time John Sculley, the Apple CEO of the time, by the time he was pushed out of the company, the company had something like 70 product lines. No company can survive by making so many products, especially if they’re not selling.

Shane Parrish: They couldn’t say no to anything. Steve’s not checked out, but not as involved at NeXT as he was. Apple’s thinking of buying BeOS as a means of saving themselves, I think is my recollection of this. But then, a voicemail changes everything.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. This is one of the luckier stories in Silicon Valley history. If this story had gone any differently, the story of Apple would have not happened. Apple might have literally gone out of business. There would be no iPhone, no iPod, none of this would’ve happened.

Apple was entering a crisis, and the crisis was on many fronts. They had released a product, a laptop that was exploding. The batteries would ignite on fire. They had to recall it. There was a product called the Newton, a stylist pen product, and it wasn’t catching on. It was buggy. It was disorganized. Apple was having failure after failure across the board.

And one of the things that they had to upgrade was their operating system, the core of their product, because without a good operating system, your computer is just dead wood.

And so, I don’t know if, Shane, you used Apple computers back in the ’90s, if you remember what it was like, there would be crashes, and freezes, and they had this thing called the spinning beach ball of death, a little beach ball thing that shows up, and it just spins around, and around, and around.

And it means that the computer was trying to load something, but it just can’t load it, so it sits there for an hour, and does nothing. It really was a miserable experience trying to use an Apple computer in the year 1996. And so, Gil Amelio was the CEO appointed to come in and turn around the company. He also brought in another executive named Ellen Hancock, who was the CTO. And they were both looking together at a new operating system.

How can we stop this silly crashing operating system, this beach ball of death? Nothing works. How can we upgrade this? And the only way that we can do it is by acquiring another company. They only had a number of months until bankruptcy. Apple was going to go bankrupt eventually. It was hemorrhaging cash. And so, they had to do something quickly, and they had to acquire an operating system.

Shane Parrish: Apple looks to buy the competitor basically to NeXTSTEP, which is BeOS.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. And that is run by none other than the greatest rival to Steve Jobs, Jean-Louis Gassée, the same man who tattled on him about trying to oust the CEO, and got him pushed out of Apple in the end.

This is a moment of revenge for Steve if he can find a way to get his OS back into Apple. Apple wasn’t really looking at NeXT Computer. Nobody was really taking it that seriously. There was an employee, a manager named Garrett Rice, who was a middle of the line manager at NeXT.

He and his friends were watching all of this happen, and they knew that their technology was superior. And they were just so annoyed, because they had spent years, and years, and years, all those long nights, creating this beautiful operating system. And meanwhile, Apple goes over to Gassee’s company, BeOS, and they say, “Hey, we want to acquire you guys.” But, they knew that NeXT technology was so much better.

Garrett picks up the phone just randomly and says, “Okay, I’m going to call Apple, and just see what happens.” He calls an executive, and remember, this is a middle manager. He gives him a pitch. He says, “You’ve got to look at this because this is cutting edge.” The executive calls back and says, “I’m leaving Apple, but you should talk to our chief technology officer, Ellen Hancock. Here’s her number.” He calls her, leaves the voicemail, and to his surprise, she calls back and she says, “Okay, we want to take a look at this, this NeXTSTEP OS.” And from there, that’s where the story just turns around.

Shane Parrish: And so, Apple ends up buying NeXTSTEP. Does he go back and become CEO? What happens?

Geoffrey Cain: It’s not that simple. It’s a winding road back. Steve actually did not want to return to Apple. Apple came to him, they said, “We want your operating system. We think that this is going to be a major acquisition.” And Steve was thinking, “Well, I just want to stick with Pixar, because I really loved Toy Story. The IPO was great.”

Steve agreed finally I will return to Apple, but only as a part-time advisor. And he said, “I don’t want a fancy title. I don’t want a fancy office. I’m just going to be an advisor. I’ll go around Apple. I’ll meet with engineers. I’ll give them feedback, but I’m not going to lead the company. And if I decide I don’t like this, I’m going to ditch Apple. I’m just going to go back to Pixar.”

Shane Parrish: Wow.

Geoffrey Cain: When Steve returned, they wanted to set up a ceremony for him. He would arrive in a helicopter, and the Apple employees would all hold up little digital candles to recognize the return of their great saint Steve Jobs.

Shane Parrish: Because the Apple employees, from their perspective, it’s like our hero is coming back to save us.

Geoffrey Cain: Yes. They didn’t know at the time that he was reluctant and unsure. Steve comes back, and he just sees disaster. It’s a disaster zone. He talked about this. All of his executives talked about it. Just nothing worked at Apple. Literally, you would try to get anything done, and it would just get killed by bureaucracy in fighting competition. Steve quickly realized that he had to put his people in Apple.

Even if Steve was not the CEO, he wanted his hardware, and his software chief at NeXT Computer to run hardware and software at Apple, because those are the only two people who could turn around the company. And so, his people, John Rubinstein, Avie Tevanian, two legends in the story of Apple, Steve put them in power, and finally they were able to make good decisions.

Shane Parrish: How does he get sucked into running it?

Geoffrey Cain: He was so reluctant. At one point, he sold almost all of his Apple shares out of frustration with leadership there. And a guy who wants to return and take over the company doesn’t sell all of his shares.

And he even said later, he said, “The reason I did it is, because I was in a fit of depression. I didn’t like Apple, what was happening here,” so he cashed out. He said, “Goodbye.” And he was thinking of going back to Pixar. Interestingly, the one person who tried to pull him back in was Larry Ellison, a guy in the news a lot now.

Larry Ellison was Steve’s best friend in the sense that Steve … Steve didn’t have a lot of friends, but this was one of the few people that you could call a friend of Steve’s. The pair were similar in a lot of ways, strong personalities, force of will.

And Larry wanted to set up a hostile takeover of Apple. He thought it would be such a thrilling experience, just a thrill to be able to go into Apple, and force a board vote, and get the shareholders behind you, and just take over Apple from the current CEO and save it.

That was his vision. But, Steve differed from that because Steve, when he was younger, would’ve gone along with that, would’ve said, “Yeah, of course, Apple’s mine. I’m going to go back in, fire the CEO, and put myself in as CEO.” But, the older Steve realized that the hostile strategy was not going to work, because he was entering unfriendly ground.

Shane Parrish: Right.

Geoffrey Cain: He was no longer going to be the saint of Apple. The angelic halo was going to disappear. And people were going to question him and say, “Well, why is Steve Jobs partaking in a hostile takeover of a company he co-founded?” Steve decided that he wanted to be welcomed back if he was going to return, and he did return.

Shane Parrish: He wanted to be wanted.

Geoffrey Cain: He wanted to be wanted. He wanted to be seen. He wanted people to see his vision and his products. He did not want to go in there anymore and pointlessly yell at people. And don’t get me wrong, he was still difficult.

But, having been through this crucible of NeXT Computer, he realized that you do have to step back, and you have to let events unfold as they need to, rather than you trying to seize control at every moment.

Shane Parrish: He’s still difficult to work with, but why do so many talented people stay with him?

Geoffrey Cain: He brought the best out of them. And they all said that, they said working for him was the hardest experience of my life, but it was also the most beautiful. They said, “Yeah, I had hard nights. I cried. I suffered. I didn’t see my family for days sometimes. I was at the office sleeping on the sofa.”

But, they said, “Yeah, it was the hardest time of my life. But, Steve was special because he could reach into my soul, and he could bring the best out of me. He looked at me, he looked through me,” they would say, “And he would reach right in, and give me the level of creativity that I wanted, that I didn’t realize I had inside me.”

Shane Parrish: I think that’s fascinating, because I just think about this, right, and it’s like his reputation externally for being really tough on people. And then, internally, he was really tough on people, but they stayed. And I have been trying to think about this in my head.

And one of the ways that I’ve framed this is that he had standards for himself and other people that they couldn’t see. And because they couldn’t see these standards, they were higher than they knew they were capable of. But, by pushing people towards higher standards, he got the best out of them.

Geoffrey Cain: Right. Steve had high standards for himself in the sense that he saw himself as somebody who was going to shape the future of the world. He was going to shape the arc of history. He always had these grandiose expectations. But, at NeXT, what he learned was how to bring good expectations to the people around him, to lift them up rather than tear them down.

Once he transitioned to that stage, and realized that lifting others up, people who do great work, once you bring them into that pressure cooker of talent, the incubator of talent, you bring them in, you put them in a room together, you force them to defend their ideas, and you acknowledge them when they do great work.

There’s a famous interview that just resurfaced recently, and it shows Steve reflecting. It’s the year 1996 after all this drama at NeXT and Pixar. He’s finally coming out of the wilderness, and he’s reflecting, and he’s saying, “Something interesting happens when you’re the CEO leading great people, when you have talent around. The pyramid gets inverted. You’re no longer the boss up top telling people what to do. You are the CEO at the bottom, and your job is to allow your talent to do their best, and to keep them around, because your talent, they can get another job in a minute, so you better do what you can to keep them around, or else you’re going to fail.”

Shane Parrish: If you had to summarize the lessons he learned, what are the key lessons that he learned through this period at NeXT?

Geoffrey Cain: The key lessons, the first is trusting your people. The second is the importance of bending your vision, knowing when to stick to your guns, and knowing when you need to back off, and you need to work with the world around you. Steve originally thought that a great idea was what mattered. If you build the great computer, the world will find it, and they will buy it, and you will be a success. But, that’s not how the world works.

He realized that you need to work with your rivals sometimes. He called Microsoft’s Bill Gates ‘The arch enemy’. This is the first thing he did when he returned to Apple as CEO, signed a deal with them. They were going to produce Word for Apple, and they were going to invest $150 million to save Apple. The younger Steve would’ve never done that because that would’ve been a cardinal sin against the Holy Church of Apple. The Apple fans already saw it as controversial.

Shane Parrish: That saved Apple, that $150 million.

Geoffrey Cain: It was the injection that kept them afloat, and it saved them. If that had not happened, they would’ve run out of money. This is Steve, the pragmatist. This is Steve who’s learned through repeat failures that you have to work with people. Even if you disagree with them, even if you think their taste sucks, and you think that their products are terrible, if they have a pot of money, and they can help you, you have to do the handshake.

You have to find a way out, because he learned that to achieve his hardware, software unity, to achieve that total control, you have to build scale first. And how do you build scale? You make deals with people. You get investors, you get distributors, but you have to make concessions. You can’t do everything exactly as you start out planning to.

Shane Parrish: Talk to me about the Gates/Jobs rivalry, and what you learned about that, and any cool stories you heard.

Geoffrey Cain: These two guys, they would take a crap on each other at any chance they could. They would get out in public, and they would insult each other’s ideas and say, “This is stupid.” What was the disagreement that they were having? One of them, Bill Gates, believed that software should fundamentally be flexible and available to everybody. It should be on every computer regardless of the hardware. That’s what Windows was.

Windows was the operating system that loaded on almost every PC in the world, and that’s why Bill Gates was so successful. But, Steve Jobs was the polar opposite in almost every way. And he believed that beautiful technology has to be within the walled garden. You can make beautiful software, but it has to be on your beautiful hardware too.

This was a theme in this entire period, Steve and Bill sparring back and forth over whose idea was better, and who’s going to win in the end? And interestingly, if you were sitting around in 1995, this is the year that Windows 95 came out, major business success, you would’ve thought that the open system makes more sense. Bill Gates and Microsoft are the future. But, if you’re sitting around in 2026, and looking at all this, it looks more like the closed ecosystem, the Apple ecosystem is actually the success.

Shane Parrish: It’s amazing how they’re both very different visions of the future, and they’re right maybe at different times.

Geoffrey Cain: That’s one of the themes that I stumbled upon in this book, because I would find, oh, well, the common wisdom of today, it didn’t really apply 30 years ago. There was a different world, different system. And that wisdom in the 1990s, it didn’t really apply in the 1980s. As you go back through history, and you look at the way humans use their technology, there’s always a different system.

It’s not so much the open or closed question that matters. It’s more about the logic of the system that you’re building. If the system favors an open approach, then the people who win in the end are going to be open developers. If it’s closed, then the moment matters as much as the technology itself. Yeah, right now, we’re in more of a closed ecosystem moment. Apple is a $4 trillion company. The iPhone is everywhere. But, in 10 years, the common wisdom of the day, maybe with AI coming in, it’s going to look totally different.

Shane Parrish: Are there any fun moments in the Steve Jobs, Bill Gates rivalry where they prank each other or poke each other intentionally that come to mind?

Geoffrey Cain: Steve Jobs was signing a deal with IBM, which was the deal of a lifetime, because Steve was going to put his NeXTSTEP operating system on millions of IBM computers. Now, this is really important, because Windows, run by Bill Gates is the operating system that’s just starting to emerge as the dominant one, and they’re also on IBM computers.

This is a really interesting moment, because Steve actually had an opportunity to literally change the technology world. It would all look different today if he had continued with IBM. We would be using computers today with NeXTSTEP operating systems rather than Apple.

Bill Gates is threatened by this, because Windows is on IBM, and this is the empire he’s trying to build. The moment Steve Jobs starts moving into that realm, Bill Gates freaks out, and he’s like, “I got to see a demonstration. I don’t know what it is that you’re doing, but this is not a good idea.” He does not like the idea of Steve Jobs’ software working with IBM.

Now, luckily for Bill, he didn’t have to do much, because Steve Jobs blew up the deal anyway, the deal of a lifetime that would have made NeXT an absolute killer success. Steve just walked away, because he didn’t like IBM. He thought they were corporate, and stuffy, and he didn’t like their 120-page contract. And so, IBM just got fed up and they said, “Okay, we’re not working with this guy anymore. Let’s just work with Gates because he’s easy to work with.”

Bill Gates is perhaps the luckiest man alive, because if Steve were not this pigheaded at this time, Bill Gates might have had a serious competition. In 1988, Steve released the Cube computer, and this is Steve’s big return. It’s going to be like his moment where he’s returning to that stage. It’s been a few years since he was ousted from Apple. And now, finally, we get to see Steve Jobs, the Prince of Tech in the flesh again, releasing this beautiful Cube computer.

What’s the first thing that Bill Gates does? He goes up in front of the press, and he literally says, “I’m not developing software for this. I’m going to piss on it.” And Bill Gates just goes on this tirade in public and says, “Steve Jobs doesn’t know what he’s doing. It’s just a cube. It’s painted black.” He says, “I could do that too. I could paint my cubes black. Why is that a special thing?”

One of the things I found in my research, turns out this has never been published, but Bill Gates actually wrote an apology to Steve, but it was like a non-apology apology.

I read the letter, and it was really hilarious, because he’s like, “Dear Steve, you saw the comments that I made in the media in which I called your product stupid and silly. I just want to apologize for that. But, I also want to let you know that everything you’ve done is wrong here, and all this tech is not going to work. And I think your idea is stupid, but I’m sorry anyway.”

Shane Parrish: It must have taken a lot for Jobs to go to Gates when he was turning around, when he was saving Apple, to go to his arch rival, his nemesis, if you will, and ask for money.

Geoffrey Cain: It took a lot, and it was extremely controversial even within Apple, because for the Apple faithful to turn to their greatest villain, Bill Gates, the man who is the 1984 big brother to them, that’s how they see him.

Shane Parrish: It shows you how far he’d grown.

Geoffrey Cain: Yeah. It shows you the new Steve. He realized that these petty fights are pretty pointless. You can go up there and take pot shots at each other in public, but that’s not going to drive sales. It’s not going to make your product more interesting to people. It’s certainly a spectacle, and it’s theater, but ultimately, it’s the product that matters. And if you don’t have a good product, nobody’s going to care about all that.

Shane Parrish: How do we go from the transition between Steve’s back, he’s part-time, he’s trying to stay out of things, or not be involved. He’s selling his Apple stock to Steve running as interim CEO, which he never relinquished.

Geoffrey Cain: The summer of ’97 is a time of deep reflection for Steve, because he doesn’t want to be the CEO yet. He still loves Pixar. His wife, Laurene, has been opposed to him returning to Apple in the first place.

One of the things that executives told me at Apple this time is that one of them actually said this phrase, “Apple kills you. It’s such a stressful place that you’re going to grow old, you’re going to get sick, and you’re going to die young.” An executive told me that’s how bad Apple was in 1997. Everybody around Steve doesn’t think that he’s going to become the CEO. And finally, it was a phone call to Andy Grove, one of his very earliest mentors, CEO of Intel, he calls him at an odd hour, and just says, “Hey, Andy, I want to talk. We’ve been interviewing these candidates, CEO of Apple. We don’t really like any of them.”

And Andy Grove has a reputation for being a straight shooter. He cuts right through. He doesn’t hide his feelings. And he literally told Steve, “Steve, I don’t give a shit about Apple.” And that was that. It hit Steve really hard. And Steve told this story later. He said, “That’s when I realized that I do give a shit about Apple.” He realized the contrast couldn’t be starker. His mentor doesn’t care, but he was jolted and he thought, “Well, wait, I do care. This is my love. This is my company.” And so, he said, “I will become the interim CEO.” And that’s what happens.

Shane Parrish: Oh, that’s crazy.

Geoffrey Cain: October 1997, Steve Jobs is appointed the interim CEO of Apple, and returns to enormous fanfare. And we all know how the story ends.

Shane Parrish: And the rest is history.

Geoffrey Cain: The rest is history.

Shane Parrish: And one of the first things he does when he takes over as CEO is kill 70 of these 80 projects.

Geoffrey Cain: Right, right. He killed 70% of Apple projects upon taking over as the interim CEO. He wasn’t even the full CEO yet. And Steve decided he wanted to be called the iCEO. This is the first ever ‘i’ mention in Apple, the predecessor to the iPod and the iPhone. And so, Steve, as the iCEO, decides we’re killing 70% of projects that are just not working.

He brings in his operating system from NeXT with its beautiful programming, the objects, the new technology, and he turns it into the foundation for everything that comes after. It becomes the software that’s going to power Apple’s Renaissance. It goes on to lead to the building of the iPhone, the iPad.

It percolates throughout Apple, and it becomes the basis for anything that’s made at Apple. You have to look at the NeXTSTEP software to understand where Apple is today. And I literally, just recently, I asked one of the very senior Apple software designers from the time who knew Steve, I asked him, how many products today at Apple really come from NeXT? And he looked at me, and looked like he thought it was a funny question. And he said, “All of them.”

Shane Parrish: That’s crazy. One of the things that I don’t think gets enough attention with Steve is the role that Laurene played in his life. Talk to me about that.

Geoffrey Cain: Laurene was the woman who softened him. Steve, as a younger man, was always a bit aimless in his personal life. He knew that he wanted a family, that he wanted to settle down, but there was a hole in his soul, and he just couldn’t find that. But, Laurene had a way with him.

And everybody who was around the couple during these years recounted that, just how Steve, by giving birth to their son together, Reed, by raising a family together, and having that presence of Laurene in his day-to-day life, he became less of a professional robot, somebody who goes to work every day, and somebody who started to treasure simple family moments.

Shane Parrish: He had a child before Laurene.

Geoffrey Cain: And treated her horribly.

Shane Parrish: When did that change? How did that change?

Geoffrey Cain: Lisa was his first daughter, and born with a different woman, but Steve denied paternity, and refused to help her take care of her. Even said at one point that she would be disinherited. But, after they met Laurene, it was in the 1990s that she was brought back into the fold, and they started to repair their relationship.

Shane Parrish: Laurene clearly played an influence in that, or was it the birth of Reed?

Geoffrey Cain: It was both. Laurene created structure in his life, a structure outside of Apple. And I think that Steve, as he got older, was able to not just be an Apple guy anymore, but was able to decenter his life among family, among NeXT, among Pixar. He had different parts of his identity, so he wasn’t going to suddenly crash if one part went wrong.

Shane Parrish: Let’s switch gears a little bit, and do more rapid fire answers.

Geoffrey Cain: All right.

Shane Parrish: Talk to me about the shithead hero rollercoaster.

Geoffrey Cain: You were either a hero one day or a shithead on another. Steve would walk into a room. If he liked your idea, you were a hero. But, the next day, he would change his mind, and say you’re a shithead, because suddenly, he doesn’t like it.

Shane Parrish: Did he like small talk?

Geoffrey Cain: No, he came right in, and he would state the vision, and make things clear. He did have one thing that he did. He would walk around and ask people what they were working on randomly, and he didn’t want them to defend themselves. He just wanted to hear what they were working on, and that’s where a lot of great ideas came from.

Shane Parrish: How did he keep so many talented people working for him?

Geoffrey Cain: He brought the best out of them. He inspired them, and he pushed them to their very limit.

Shane Parrish: How did he make decisions?

Geoffrey Cain: He told people to talk back to him. Talk back and disagree with me, and we’ll find the answer through disagreement.

Shane Parrish: When did he learn focus?

Geoffrey Cain: When he was at rock bottom. He learned that you can’t do everything just because you think it’s a neat idea. You have to focus your efforts on what will be profitable.

Shane Parrish: Did he have friends?

Geoffrey Cain: No, no real friends. Larry Ellison was the closest person to a friend.

Shane Parrish: Did he ever apologize to people?

Geoffrey Cain: Yes, interestingly. He would throw them on the hero shithead rollercoaster, and then he would occasionally apologize a few days later for being so nasty to them.

Shane Parrish: Would he do it in public, or would he do it in private?

Geoffrey Cain: He would write them a letter.

Shane Parrish: Was he clear with apologies, or did you guys see any of these letters? What did they look like?

Geoffrey Cain: Those specific letters, I didn’t see those, but people recounted them to me. Steve apologized in writing, and he would be specific about the apology, but he also expected the conversation to be over.

Shane Parrish: That was it?

Geoffrey Cain: That was it. We’re done.

Shane Parrish: We’re done. Did he have empathy for other people?

Geoffrey Cain: Yes.

Shane Parrish: That surprises me.

Geoffrey Cain: He learned empathy. He lined up top flight medical care for employees who were suffering.

Shane Parrish: But, not himself.

Geoffrey Cain: But, not himself. He learned empathy for others, but he wouldn’t give empathy to himself.

Shane Parrish: One thing that doesn’t make sense to me though is it sounds like Steve learned to learn from feedback, and people around him during these time at NeXT. And yet, when it came to his own medical treatment, he insisted on doing things his way despite the advice of doctors, friends, loved ones, family. How do you reconcile that?

Geoffrey Cain: Steve didn’t change completely. He was still the same person at his core, and he still had the reality distortion field, but that’s the mindset that goes behind his decision not to get treatment. He consulted a psychic about his medical condition. He relied on holistic vegan foods to try to cure his cancer, but that’s not how it works. But, that is classic Steve. Steve learned the power of inspiring the people around him, but he never completely learned to be 100% honest with himself.

Shane Parrish: If there are key takeaways from your book that people could use in their everyday life, either at work, to get ahead, or in life to live a better life, what would they be?

Geoffrey Cain: If Steve Jobs was at rock bottom, and failing, and Steve Jobs went through 12 years in the wilderness, and he came out of it, and became the Steve Jobs we know, just think about how he did that, and how maybe our problems, our everyday problems are maybe not as vast as what he was facing.

Shane Parrish: Reading your book, it struck me that he was naturally resilient, but he had to learn discipline.

Geoffrey Cain: That’s exactly right. He was resilient in the face of failure after failure. Once he learned discipline, his resilience became the foundation for his success.

Shane Parrish: What can we learn from his resilience? How do you teach people to be that resilient? He persisted. He was so determined.

Geoffrey Cain: If you’re in hard times, you treat it as the foundation for what might come after. That’s where the resilience comes from. If you’re only focused in the current moment, then it’s easy to give up. But, failure could be the foundation for success later.

Shane Parrish: One thing we were talking about before we started recording that I think is massively misunderstood, but if you hold a microscope up to anybody, you’re going to see even exceptional people, people that we hold up as heroes are human, and they have flaws. And it is in part those flaws that make them heroes, and it’s in part the journey that they’ve been on.

And I want to thank you for this conversation, because this is a part of Steve Jobs’ life that very few people know about, or understand how this walk through the wilderness, if you want to call it that, or the hero’s journey, if you will, actually led to him being the person that we remember.

Geoffrey Cain: Absolutely. And I want to thank you too, Shane. That was a great conversation. In the wilderness years, those are hard years, but that’s where many great leaders have learned to become who they need to be.

Shane Parrish: What is success for you?

Geoffrey Cain: Success is waking up in the morning, and having the family and the friends around you who really make life great. It’s walking into a coffee shop, and being able to sit down, and enjoy yourself, and enjoy the moment, enjoy whatever it is that you’re doing, whether you are writing a book, or building a company, or making a movie. It’s being able to just sit down, and to do that, and to enjoy these moments as they come.
